## Gharb Jabal Marrah Locality, Central Darfur State

Nertiti town and IDP camps · Guildo · Quila · Kutrum · Golol

FINAL REPORT - Data collection 7-9 July 2026 · Report date 21 July 2026

Participating organizations: Save the Children International (SCI), World Relief (WR), Danish Refugee Council (DRC), Islamic Relief Worldwide (IRW), United Peace Organization (UPO), Aid Point, TDO, Jabal Marra Charity Organization for Rural Development (JMCO), Deriba Center for Environmental Studies (DCES). ## Summary of key findings

- The five assessed locations host an estimated 39,261 households (235,566 people), with roughly nine in ten concentrated in Nertiti town and its IDP camps. Individual totals are derived using a uniform assumption of six persons per household. These working figures must be reconciled with DTM and locality authorities before use in targeting or coverage calculations.
- According to the assessment, food assistance is the leading priority along the Zalingei-Nertiti corridor. Humanitarian presence has grown along the main road, while "second-belt" communities off it - including Guildo, Quila, Kutrum and Golol - remain largely underserved. New arrivals were reported into Kutrum, Quila and Golol.
- Services are contracting as needs deepen: the closure of donor-funded projects affects 39 health facilities in Central Darfur (services suspended in 23 and reduced in a further 7), and cholera response kits are in critical shortage across the Jebel Marra area.

## Key findings from the household interviews (n=168, 7-9 July):

- The assessment found simultaneous, not sequential, needs: 89% of households could meet basic needs only partially or not at all; 65% faced severe food shortage or days without food in the past week; 94% reported overcrowded, damaged/leaking or unsafe shelter; 85% could access essential healthcare only partially or not at all; and 57% had insufficient water.
- Assistance coverage is limited and, where received, largely inadequate: 40% of households received no assistance of any kind in the previous three months, and of the 101 households that did receive support, only 4 said it fully met their urgent needs.

- Affordability is the dominant reported constraint: insufficient money (95%) and high prices (75-77%) lead the barrier profiles. Cash was preferred by 54% of assessed households, but preference alone does not establish feasibility; market supply, trader liquidity, prices, transfer value, access and protection conditions require verification.
- Golol presents a distinct protection and access profile: 69% of assessed households felt unsafe most or all of the time, 6 of the 7 severe movement-restriction reports in the whole dataset came from Golol, 56% were sheltering in public or abandoned buildings, and 56% practiced open defecation. Delivery there must be adapted to movement constraints and safely verified first.
- School non-attendance was high in the assessed sample: about two-thirds of school-age girls (65%) and boys (66%) in applicable households were not attending, with school costs the dominant barrier (73%).

## 1. Background and rationale

West Jebel Marra hosts both protracted and recent displacement. ABC coordination records from May 2026 list 17 IDP camps in the wider Jebel Marra, including sites in and around Nertiti, with Al-Salam and Khor Ramla among the established displacement reference sites. In the same period, participants in coordination discussions flagged - pending validation - that IDPs in Nertiti/Al Salam were sheltering in schools and public buildings.

From 5 to 9 July 2026, an OCHA-led mission (OCHA, ABC, WFP and TGH) met humanitarian partners in Nertiti and reviewed a consolidated mapping of activities along the Zalingei-Nertiti corridor. Participants acknowledged increased presence along the main road but stressed that communities in the second belt remain largely underserved. Food assistance was identified by participants as the leading priority because many IDPs remain unregistered and therefore excluded from assistance, and Kutrum, Quila and Golol were highlighted as receiving new arrivals. SCI and DRC undertook to compile a list of locations that received limited or no assistance over the past year, and OCHA and ABC agreed to facilitate a Rapid Needs Assessment - the present exercise.

## 2. Objectives

- Establish a household-level, multi-sector needs baseline across the five locations.
- Quantify severity by sector and identify drivers of exclusion from assistance.
- Surface location-specific variation between Nertiti town and camps and the four second-belt villages.
- Provide sectors and clusters with evidence for prioritization, targeting and resource mobilization during the rainy season.
- Strengthen the shared evidence base for follow-up and support fundraising efforts.

## 3. Methodology and coverage

The assessment is a multi-sector, household-level exercise administered on KoboToolbox by mixed inter-agency enumeration teams, with 190 household interviews allocated across the five locations. The allocation deliberately oversampled the four smaller locations to support directional location analysis. Overall percentages are unweighted and therefore describe the assessed sample, not the population distribution across the five locations (Table 1).

Data were collected on 7-9 July 2026 (established from device timestamps; the manual date field contained device-default errors and was not used). Of 170 submissions received, 2 were excluded on supervisor review, leaving 168 usable interviews - 88% of the 190-interview target. Of the retained interviews, 158 (94%) were conducted in person and 10 by phone. Interview duration was not calculated from start/end metadata because delayed form finalization or syncing produced implausible elapsed times.

## Limitations

The design is a rapid quota exercise sized for operational insight, not statistical representativeness. Village samples of 16-28 households support directional findings only - Golol (n=16), Kutrum (n=22) and Guildo (n=24) percentages can shift substantially with a few interviews, and location differences should be treated as validation priorities rather than rankings. Population denominators are unverified working estimates; recall and courtesy bias apply. Administrative coding inconsistencies were standardized using settlement names during cleaning. Sector indicators are reported at location level; disaggregation by displacement status is derivable from the household dataset and available on request for sector targeting. The questionnaire did not capture a full age- and sex-disaggregated household roster, so under-five, adolescent and adult female and male caseloads for Education, Child Protection and Nutrition should be derived using agreed demographic ratios during reconciliation with DTM, and an age/sex roster should be added in future rounds.

## 4. Situation overview and secondary data

Locality-level planning figures used in ABC prioritization (DTM-informed, January 2026) put the West Jebel Marra locality population at approximately 124,000, with around 68,000 people estimated in IPC Phase 3 or above. The working estimates consolidated for this assessment - 235,566 people across five locations - substantially exceed that baseline, but the figures may differ in geographic scope, reference date and estimation method. The assessment total also applies a uniform six-person household conversion. Reconciliation with DTM, locality authorities and partner caseload lists is required before either figure is used for population-based targeting or coverage calculations.

<!-- image -->

Secondary evidence compiled in the assessment analysis annex situates these locations within the wider crisis: IOM DTM recorded around 9.58 million IDPs across Sudan as of 30 September 2025, with Central Darfur hosting about a tenth of the national caseload; DTM later recorded 138,194 people (30,159 households) displaced from El Fasher town and surrounding villages between 26 October 2025 and 1 March 2026, and UNICEF separately identified onward movement beyond Tawila to Nertiti and Golo; the September 2025 IPC analysis estimated around 713,000 people (59% of the analysed Central Darfur population) in IPC Phase 3 or above, while the June 2026 IPC update retained the previous Central Darfur analysis because no new outcome data were available and issued no June 2026-January 2027 projection for the state; and on 17 June 2026 the Health Cluster warned that a funding interruption could affect 45 health facilities or services in Central Darfur after June. The assessment findings connect directly to this picture: 27% of assessed households reported displacement from, or hosting members displaced from, El Fasher.

The response context is contracting as needs deepen. The Health Cluster identified 45 facilities or services in Central Darfur at risk beyond June 2026, and local coordination tracking reports the closure of donor-funded projects already affecting 39 facilities, with services suspended in 23 and reduced in a further seven; the overlap between the two counts requires confirmation. Health partners reported a critical shortage of cholera response kits across the Jebel Marra area and no consolidated preparedness-and-supplies mapping available at the time. They also expected road access from Zalingei to deteriorate as the rains progressed, with consequences for medical resupply and prepositioning. OCHA and ABC have agreed to convene a monthly hybrid, locality-level multi-sector coordination meeting to close the information and escalation gap.

## 5. Sector findings

## Household and displacement profile

Respondents were 71% female. Assessed households were 52% IDPs, 35% permanent residents, 8% returnees, and 5% seasonal returnees; 58% were interviewed in IDP sites (camps, informal sites, collective and reception centers) and 42% in host communities. Median household size was 7 (interquartile range 5-9). Vulnerability was widespread: 51% of households included a pregnant or lactating woman, 33% an older person, 31% a person with disability, and 20% a person with chronic illness; only 10% reported none of the listed specific needs.

<!-- image -->

Source: NIRNA household dataset, 7-9 July 2026 (n=168)

Conflict or insecurity at origin drove displacement for 79% of households answering the movement module. El Fasher-linked households - displaced from El Fasher or hosting members displaced from it - made up 27% overall, rising to 36% in Nertiti town and camps, with a median of 4 linked members. Arrivals within the last 12 months appear almost entirely in the Nertiti (and to a lesser extent Guildo) interviews; the Kutrum, Quila and Golol interviews captured 5% or fewer recent arrivals, so the newarrival movements reported there by participants are not yet visible in this dataset - a coverage caveat and verification point, not evidence of absence. A third of households (32%) expressed intent to return; among the 146 who answered the barriers question, insecurity (71%), shelter/housing (57%), and food (42%) ranked highest.

Regarding the most pressing humanitarian need, households put food first by a wide margin, followed by education, household NFIs, and health care. Overall, 89% could meet basic needs only partially (51%) or not at all (38%); insufficient money (95%) and high prices (75%) dominate the barrier profile. On modality, 54% preferred cash, 20% in-kind, and 10% a mixed package; 76% reported no safety concern around receiving assistance, with theft/extortion risk (12%) and movement risk to service points (10%) the main exceptions to mitigate. These preferences do not replace a market-feasibility, transfer-value or protection analysis.

<!-- image -->

Source: NIRNA household dataset 7-9 July 2026 (n=168)

## Food Security and Livelihoods

According to participants in the July 2026 coordination discussions, food assistance is the leading priority along the corridor: many IDPs remain unregistered and excluded from general food assistance, and new arrivals into Kutrum, Quila and Golol are adding pressure on already-stretched hostcommunity stocks as the rainy season begins.

The assessment found food to be the most consistent immediate concern: only 6% of households described food access in the past week as adequate, while 39% reported severe shortage and a further 26% reported days with no food at all. Most adults ate twice a day (79%) and 17% only once; children's meal counts were similar (80% twice, 8% once, among 147 valid responses). Main food sources were own production (40%), market purchase (25%) and humanitarian assistance (15%), with 15% relying on gifts or borrowing. Lack of money (95%) and high food prices (77%) overwhelm all other access barriers; no household reported a non-functioning market. This is a respondent perception, not a market assessment of supply depth, trader liquidity, price volatility or supply-chain continuity.

Coping is already eroding welfare and protection: 62% reduced portions, and 58% skipped meals in the past week; 24% reported child labor and 11% early marriage as coping strategies; 15% of adults reduced their own food for children, and 13% bought food on credit. Livelihoods rest on daily wage labor (48%) and crop or livestock farming (29%), with 9% reporting no income source at all; lack of jobs (57%), land access (54%) and seeds and tools (49%) are the leading constraints as the planting window passes. Assistance coverage compounds the food picture: 40% of households received no assistance of any kind in the previous three months, and food assistance reached 36% (see Accountability to Affected People). Local responders are also active: Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) in Nertiti run communal kitchens with DRC support, and ERR and mutual aid group presence in the second-belt villages should be mapped into coverage planning.

<!-- image -->

Location-specific findings: within the assessed sample, severe shortage or no-food days were reported by 72% in Nertiti, 71% in Guildo (where all 24 assessed households named food as a top need) and 36% in Kutrum. These descriptive differences require validation.

## WASH

Cholera risk rises with the rains while response kits are in critical shortage across the Jebel Marra area. Water and sanitation coverage in the second belt was previously undocumented; this exercise provides structured household-level findings for the five locations.

Half of households relied mainly on a borehole or handpump, but 40% used surface water (24%) or an unprotected well (16%) - the core of waterborne-disease risk as the rains progress. Fifty-seven percent reported insufficient water for household needs, and 27% travelled more than 60 minutes one way; long queues (55%), limited availability (44%), and lack of containers (40%) were the main barriers. Quality concerns were widespread - suspected contamination 54%, turbidity 40%, diarrhea worries 35% - yet 66% never treat drinking water (96% in Quila).

<!-- image -->

Source: NIRNA household dataset, 7-9 July 2026 (n=168)

Sanitation and hygiene mirror the water picture: 55% used shared latrines, 23% practiced open defecation, and 75% said available latrines were not safe, private or usable. Only 8% had water and soap for handwashing (65% water only). Requested hygiene items were soap (88%), water containers (74%), treatment supplies (55%), and menstrual hygiene items (43%). Two-thirds of households identified water-collection routes (66%) and latrines (64%) as places where women and girls feel unsafe - direct guidance for source siting, lighting and latrine standards.

Location-specific findings: water insufficiency peaks in Guildo (83%) and Kutrum (77%). Quila shows uneven water access to verify in the field - 75% report sufficient quantity, yet 11 of 28 households face journeys over 60 minutes. Golol reports no long journeys but 69% depend on unprotected or surface sources.

## Health and Nutrition

Health services across Central Darfur are affected by recent funding interruptions; partners reported that no consolidated locality-level mapping of preparedness plans, referral pathways or supplies was available at the time of assessment. Rainy-season access is expected to complicate medical resupply from Zalingei.

The assessment found an access failure already underway: essential healthcare was only partially accessible for 46% of households and not accessible for 39%; just 15% reported full access. Travel burdens are heavy - 32% are more than two hours from the nearest functioning facility. Cost of services and medicines (85%), medicine shortages (73%), distance and transport (46%), staff shortages (43%) and lack of female staff or midwives (35%) form the barrier profile. Reported concerns - symptoms and worries, not diagnoses - were dominated by fever and malaria-like illness (90%) and diarrhea/AWD (52%), the latter reinforcing the cholera-preparedness case, with maternal and reproductive health needs and mental distress each at 38%.

Nutrition findings warrant screening: in the dedicated nutrition question, 49% of households reported including a pregnant or lactating woman; among the 68 households answering the nutrition module, shortage of complementary food (74%), inadequate food for pregnant and lactating women (66%), and visible child thinness or weight loss (47%) led. Malnutrition screening or treatment was reported unavailable by 60% of all households, and 59% of the 114 households answering the vaccination question reported interrupted childhood vaccination.

Location-specific findings: All assessed households in Guildo and Quila reported only partial or no healthcare access; 62% and 64%, respectively, reported no access. These findings support outreach and mobile-service validation. Malnutrition services were reported unavailable by 82% in Quila, 77% in Kutrum and 75% in Guildo; among households answering the vaccination question, interruption was reported by 71% in Quila and 65% in Nertiti.

## Emergency Shelter and NFI

Participants in coordination discussions had flagged - pending validation - that IDPs in Nertiti/Al Salam were sheltering in schools and public buildings, and new arrivals into the villages raise shelter pressure as the rains begin.

Shelter problems are near-universal: 94% of households reported at least one serious condition - damage and leakage (65%), lack of privacy (55%) or overcrowding (46%) - and only 7% described their shelter as adequate. Enumerator observation matched the household reports, flagging rainleakage risk in 68% of shelters and lack of lighting in 52%. Households were accommodated in their own homes (38%), emergency shelters (27%), hosted arrangements (23%) and collective centers (8%); tenure risk is present but secondary (15% eviction threats, 10% rent pressure). Priority NFIs are blankets (93%), mosquito nets (75%), sleeping mats (64%), water containers (60%), solar lamps (52%) and plastic sheeting (45%) - the core NFI package ahead of peak rains. Firewood is the cooking fuel for 96% of households, tying fuel collection to the protection risks reported below.

On the schools-sheltering question, the assessment did not find this pattern in the Nertiti town and camps interviews: no assessed household there was living in a public building or school. It did find it elsewhere - 9 of 16 Golol households were in public or abandoned buildings and 3 Guildo households were sheltering in a secondary school. The Nertiti/Al Salam concern still needs site-level verification, but in this assessment shelter in public buildings is a Golol and Guildo issue.

Location-specific findings: Guildo and Golol report shelter problems in every assessed household (100%); Kutrum and Nertiti report them in 95% of assessed households.

## Protection (Child Protection and GBV as AoRs)

Coordination fora have flagged thin protection service coverage beyond the main towns across the Jebel Marra area, with limited mapped referral options. The assessment provides structured householdlevel protection findings for these five locations.

Most households (80%) felt safe most of the time - but the average hides Golol, where 11 of 16 households felt unsafe most or all of the time and 6 of the dataset's 7 severe movement-restriction reports originate. Firewood and fuel collection areas were the most cited unsafe places (45%), followed by water routes and market routes (22% each) and latrine or bathing areas (21%). Households most often identified women (64%), adolescent girls (64%), older persons (56%), children under five (52%), and persons with disabilities (43%) as needing additional support.

Area-level concerns - perceptions reported at pattern level, not verified incidents - centred on child labor (52%), early marriage (39%), family separation (35%), violence or neglect against children (30%) and psychosocial distress (20%), with GBV-related safety risks named by 17%. Documentation gaps are large: 58% of households lack a national ID, and 43% lack a birth certificate, while 11 of 88 assessed IDP households (13%) reported a missing IDP registration card. The assessment did not establish whether registration status caused exclusion from assistance, so this relationship requires follow-up (see the observation findings under Accountability to Affected People). Referral awareness is fragmented: 31% did not know of any referral service, and awareness of GBV (20%) and child protection (24%) services trails that of health referrals (41%).

Location-specific findings: Golol requires an immediate, safely facilitated protection and access review before any movement-dependent service delivery is expanded there; the small sample (n=16) makes this a trigger for follow-up, not a formal severity ranking.

## Education

Where IDPs are sheltering in schools, learning continuity is at risk alongside shelter concerns. The presence of educational services in the four villages was not documented in the service mapping prior to this exercise.

Among households with school-age children answering the module, the assessment found no school attendance for girls in 65% of applicable households (n=123) and for boys in 66% (n=119). School costs and fees dominate the barriers (73%), far ahead of classroom shortage and overcrowding (33%), learning materials (24%), teachers (20%) and child labor (18%) - which links directly to the 24% of households reporting child labor as a food-coping strategy. School WASH is itself a barrier: households reported schools with no latrines (53%), unsafe or non-private latrines (42%) and no water source (41%). The support households most request is temporary classrooms (58%), learning materials (52%), and seating (38%).

Location-specific findings: boys' non-attendance was reported by 83% of applicable assessed households in Kutrum; Guildo's three households sheltering in a secondary school require joint followup between the Emergency Shelter and NFI and Education sectors.

## Accountability to Affected People (cross-cutting)

Reported registration gaps, limited assistance coverage and weak awareness of feedback channels warrant joint verification and clearer information on eligibility and entitlements.

Forty percent of households received no assistance of any kind in the previous three months (Quila 54%, Guildo and Golol 50%, Kutrum 45%, Nertiti 28%). Food assistance reached 36%, cash or vouchers 23%, shelter/NFI 18%, and health 15%. Adequacy is the deeper problem: of the 101 households that received assistance, only 4 (4%) said it fully met their urgent needs - 36% said it partially met them, and 60% said it did not at all. Awareness of feedback channels is very limited: 76% said no known mechanism was the main barrier to raising complaints. Preferred channels are community committees (51%), direct contact with aid workers (18%), help desks (10%), and women representatives (10%) - several complementary channels with visible responsiveness and closure are needed, not a single complaint box. Perceived exclusion most often concerned IDPs living within host communities (28%), older persons (21%), persons with disabilities (20%), and new arrivals (19%); these are hypotheses to check against 5W coverage, not verified incidents.

<!-- image -->

Assessment observation findings. Observations corroborate the perceived-exclusion pattern: some IDP households displaced since 2016 have not been included in food assistance because beneficiary records have not been updated and no new registration has taken place. For other assistance, such as cash and NFIs, the most vulnerable households face barriers because registration is largely managed through community leaders and sheikhs, who were reported to prioritize relatives and other influential community members.

Community members recommended that:

- organizations hold community mobilization and sensitization meetings that reach all community groups - women and men alike - rather than relying only on community leaders or sheikhs;
- beneficiary registration be carried out directly by organization staff;
- verification also be done by organization staff so that assistance reaches the most vulnerable and eligible households; and

- complaints be addressed in a timely manner, since visible responses build confidence in the complaints and feedback mechanism.

## Nertiti town and IDP camps - est. 35,621 HHs / 213,726 people (78 interviews)

The concentration point of displacement in the locality, including established sites such as Al-Salam and Khor Ramla. The assessed households are 72% IDPs and carry the arrival pressure: 36% are El Fasher-linked and a third arrived within the last 12 months. Within the assessed sample, 72% reported severe shortage or no-food days, water insufficiency runs at 62% and vaccination interruption at 65%. Seventy-two percent received assistance in the past three months - the remaining gap is the adequacy and frequency of assistance rather than reach alone, and camp/host balance should be maintained so longer-term caseloads are not displaced by arrival-focused targeting.

## Guildo village - est. 1,560 HHs / 9,360 people (24 interviews; 69% of target)

Within the assessed sample, Guildo showed consistently high reported needs across sectors: every household reported unmet or partial basic needs, every household reported a serious shelter problem, all 24 named food a top need, and 100% could access healthcare only partially (38%) or not at all (62%). Water insufficiency was reported by 83% of assessed households. Three households were sheltering in a secondary school. With 71% IDPs and the lowest interview achievement, Guildo is a priority for a follow-up mission that also closes the interview-target gap.

## Quila village - est. 911 HHs / 5,466 people (28 interviews)

A largely resident population (82% permanent residents) facing a service-access crisis rather than a displacement one: 100% reported partial or no healthcare access - including 64% reporting no access - malnutrition services were unavailable for 82%, vaccination interruption reached 71%, and 96% never treat drinking water. Water access is uneven and requires field verification: 75% report having sufficient water, while 11 of 28 households travel over an hour each way. Early marriage as a foodcoping strategy was reported by 29% of households, the highest recorded within the assessed sample - a child-protection follow-up point.

## Kutrum village - est. 721 HHs / 4,326 people (22 interviews)

The location with the highest share of returnees (36% returnees or seasonal returnees). Within the assessed sample, 36% reported severe food shortages or no-food days, 77% reported insufficient water, 95% reported shelter problems, and 83% of applicable households' boys were not attending school. Follow-up should prioritize water reliability, shelter repair during the rains, and school-cost barriers while continuing to verify food needs; the small sample does not support excluding food assistance.

## Golol village - est. 448 HHs / 2,688 people (16 interviews)

Golol faces overlapping protection and access constraints unlike the other four locations: 69% of households felt unsafe most or all of the time; six of the seven severe movement-restriction reports in the dataset came from here; 56% were sheltering in public or abandoned buildings; and 56% practiced open defecation. Water is close by (no journeys over an hour), but 69% draw from unprotected or surface sources, and nutrition and WASH each ranked among the top four priorities (56%). Basic-needs and food indicators appear less severe than elsewhere - with n=16 and constrained movement, treat that as unverified. Safe, protection-led validation comes before any expansion of movement-dependent delivery.

## Community observations recorded during the assessment

Assessment teams also recorded the following qualitative observations reported by residents and key informants:

- Health and nutrition: only one functioning facility, supported by IMC, with limited services; residents reported that no other organization has operated in their area since 2010.
- Referral: severe medical cases are transferred to Nertiti by road without dedicated transport - a journey of up to eight hours.
- Education: most schools have not opened for a long period.
- Water: most residents drink from open wells or springs, and the water is reported to be salty.
- Markets: there is no substantial local market; households move goods to and from Nertiti by camel and donkey, a journey of around eight hours.

## 7. Priorities for sector follow-up

- Second-belt coverage: extend response presence beyond the road corridor to Guildo, Quila, Kutrum and Golol - where 45-54% of assessed households received no assistance - using the SCI/DRC compilation of locations with limited or no assistance over the past year.
- Food assistance and cash/voucher support: scale food assistance and consider cash where a market assessment confirms feasibility (54% preferred cash and affordability was the dominant reported constraint).
- Health continuity and cholera preparedness: contingency planning for facilities affected by funding interruptions, pre-positioning of cholera kits and supplies before peak rains, and linkage to surveillance, referral and any oral cholera vaccination planning through the sub-national Health Cluster and WHO - prioritizing outreach and mobile services in Guildo and Quila, where all assessed households reported only partial or no healthcare access, plus vaccination catch-up and nutrition screening.
- WASH before peak rains: repair and augment priority water points (Guildo and Kutrum first), chlorination and household water treatment, community-level cholera prevention (hygiene promotion and safe-water messaging), soap and container distribution, and safe, well-lit, genderresponsive sanitation - designed around the 66% and 64% of households naming water routes and latrines as unsafe places for women and girls.
- Shelter and education interface: deliver the core NFI package ahead of peak rains (blankets, nets, mats, sheeting, lighting); verify the Nertiti/Al Salam schools-sheltering concern at site level, noting that the assessment found shelter in public buildings concentrated in Golol and Guildo, and sequence alternatives with the Emergency Shelter and NFI and Education sectors before the school term.

- Golol protection and access review: an immediate, safely facilitated protection and access verification before expanding movement-dependent delivery, with modalities adapted so assistance does not require risky travel.
- Education restart: combine school-cost relief with temporary classrooms, learning materials, seating and school WASH; link child-labor cases (24% of households as food coping) to confidential protection follow-up and household economic support.
- Accountability: establish several complementary feedback channels through community committees, aid workers, help desks and women representatives, communicate how complaints are handled, and review targeting against the perceived-exclusion findings.
- Seasonal pre-positioning and coordination: move pipeline and supply decisions forward of the expected deterioration of Zalingei-Nertiti road access; sustain the monthly hybrid locality-level multisector meeting convened by OCHA and ABC; and update ABC service mapping to administrativeunit and village level with named sector focal points, including ERR and mutual aid group presence; and circulate the ABC service-mapping (5W) extract for West Jebel Marra alongside this report so partners can see who has operational capacity in the second-belt villages.
